unit.title: The NHL and Your Person's Team

payload.prompt: Match the division or conference to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Eight NHL teams in the eastern U.S. and Canada, including Boston and Toronto.
Eight eastern teams, including the Rangers, Flyers and Penguins.
Eight Western Conference teams, including Chicago, Dallas and St. Louis.
Eight Western Conference teams, including Los Angeles, Vegas and Edmonton.
16 teams from the Atlantic and Metropolitan divisions.

explanation.summary: The NHL has four divisions (Atlantic, Metro, Central, Pacific) split into two conferences (Eastern and Western). Each conference sends eight teams to the playoffs.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Atlantic has Toronto, Tampa, Boston and five others. That division is tough.

payload.prompt: How many games in an NHL season starting 2026-27?

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026-27 season is 84 games (it was 82 before).
explanation.incorrect: The NHL added two games in 2026-27, so each team now plays 84 instead of 82. That is a long season, running from late September into April.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eighty-four games. That is a lot of nights to fall in love with a team.

payload.prompt: How did the NHL's 82 games become 84 for 2026-27?

options.text: Two extra games against divisional opponents.
Two extra games against the PWHL champion.
A longer preseason that counts in the standings.

explanation.correct: Yes. Each team plays two more games inside its division, so division rivals see each other a little more. The preseason got shorter, capped at four games.
explanation.incorrect: The two extra regular-season games are divisional games. Preseason games never count in the standings, and the league does not play the PWHL.
explanation.sayThisLine: More divisional games means more rivalry nights.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We made the playoffs as a wild card. That was so close.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The team just squeaked into the 16-team playoff field as one of two non-division winners per conference.
options.explanation: Right. Each conference sends its top three teams from each division plus two wild cards, the next-best records in the conference.

options.text: The team won their division and earned a top seed.
options.explanation: If they won the division, they would be a division winner, not a wild card. A wild card is the next-best teams in the conference.

options.text: The team is playing in a play-in tournament before the real playoffs.
options.explanation: The NHL does not use a play-in tournament. The top three in each division and the next-two best teams (wild cards) make the playoffs directly.

payload.translation: Her team finished outside the top three in its division but was one of the two next-best teams in the conference, so it earned a playoff spot as a wild card.

followUps.line: Were they in the playoff picture all season or did they sneak in late?
followUps.why: This shows whether it was a consistent run or a late-season charge. Both are exciting but tell different stories.

followUps.line: Do they face a division winner in round one, or another wild card?
followUps.why: The matchup shows how difficult their path is. Facing a division winner can be tougher because they were the best in their division.

payload.prompt: Complete the statement about the NHL season.
payload.template: An 84-game season runs from {{start}} to {{end}}, and {{playoffs}} teams make the playoffs.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026-27 regular season opens in late September and runs to April. Sixteen teams, half the league, make the playoffs.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season runs from late September to April. The top three teams in each division plus two wild cards per conference make the playoffs, so 3 x 4 + 2 x 2 = 16 teams.

payload.prompt: Which change is new for the 2026-27 NHL season?

options.text: Neck protection is required for players with no prior NHL games.
The league expanded to 36 teams.
Regular-season overtime is now ten minutes.

explanation.correct: Yes. New players must wear neck protection in 2026-27. Players already in the league can still choose. The league also added a dedicated traveling backup goalie and new contract-length limits.
explanation.incorrect: The league still has 32 teams and regular-season overtime is still five minutes. The new thing is neck protection for players with no prior NHL games.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Our new kid has to wear a neck guard this year. Feels odd, but I get why.

payload.question: What is she noticing?

options.text: New players must wear neck protection now, and she understands it is for safety.
options.explanation: Right. The 2026-27 rule requires neck protection for players with no prior NHL games, and she sees the safety point.

options.text: Veterans are banned from wearing neck guards.
options.explanation: Nobody is banned. Veterans already in the league just are not required to wear one, and many choose to.

options.text: The team is punishing the rookie for something.
options.explanation: Neck guards are a league-wide safety rule, not a team penalty. Every player with no prior NHL games has to wear one.

payload.translation: Players new to the NHL in 2026-27 must wear neck protection. It is a league safety rule, and she thinks it makes sense.

followUps.line: Are the veterans wearing them too, or just the new guys?
followUps.why: Shows you know the rule only requires it for players with no prior NHL games.

followUps.line: Does it look weird to you yet?
followUps.why: A light, curious question that lets her share her own take.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the injury history behind this rule. Asking whether it is new this year or part of a longer trend is enough.

payload.prompt: The 84-game season means fewer road games than before.

scene.alt: A team schedule showing home and road games.

explanation.correct: False. Two extra games split evenly means each team plays 42 at home and 42 on the road, one more road game than the old 41.
explanation.incorrect: More games means more of both. With 84 games, each team plays 42 at home and 42 on the road, up from 41 and 41.

payload.prompt: What is the salary cap ceiling for 2026-27?

options.text: $100 million
$104 million
$110 million

explanation.correct: Right. The upper limit is $104 million in 2026-27. The cap is a hard ceiling on what a team can spend on payroll, with only narrow tools like long-term injured reserve to work around it.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026-27 ceiling is $104 million. It tends to rise most years as league revenue grows, so always check the current figure.

payload.prompt: What defines a team's identity or personality in hockey?

options.text: Their jersey colors and logo.
Their playing style, history, and fan culture.
The city they play in.

explanation.correct: Yes. A team's identity is how they play (defensive grinders vs. high-flying offense), their history and championships, and what their fans are like.
explanation.incorrect: Team identity is more than just the uniform. It is about their personality: Are they a defensive lockdown team or an offensive machine? Do they have a proud history or are they new? What do the fans expect?

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: {{team}} is a trap team. We just shut everyone down.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: The team plays a defensive system that clogs the neutral zone and forces turnovers.
options.explanation: Right. The trap packs players into the middle of the ice so the other team cannot carry the puck through, which makes games tight and low-scoring.

options.text: The team is so bad that fans feel trapped into watching them.
options.explanation: A trap team is not bad; it is a specific defensive strategy. Successful trap teams can be hard to beat, even if games are lower-scoring.

options.text: The team plays a very physical, hitting-heavy style.
options.explanation: The trap is about positioning and clogging lanes, not physicality. Some trap teams are physical, but the trap itself is a zoning strategy.

payload.translation: Her team wins by clogging the middle of the ice to block passing lanes and force mistakes, rather than by scoring a lot of goals.

followUps.line: Is it working? Are they winning close games?
followUps.why: If the trap is effective, they should have strong playoff results and close game scores. That tells you whether the strategy is clicking.

followUps.line: Do fans think it is boring to watch?
followUps.why: Trap teams often divide opinion: some love the grit, others want more scoring. Understanding her take on it shows how she feels about her team's style.

payload.prompt: {{team}}'s identity is something they control with their roster and coaching.

explanation.correct: True. A team's identity is built intentionally through trades, signings, and the coach's system. It can evolve as the team changes.
explanation.incorrect: Teams actively shape their identity. A new coach or star acquisition can change whether {{team}} is fast and offensive or slow and defensive. It is not fixed.

payload.prompt: Match the team identity type to what it means.

pairs.definition: Team is trading veterans for picks and prospects while young players develop.
Team has stars and is built to win now; a deep playoff run is the goal.
Team is fighting for a playoff spot and could finish in or out.

explanation.summary: A team's situation shapes how fans feel about each season. A rebuilding team asks for patience, a contender has to deliver now, and a bubble team lives and dies by every point.
explanation.sayThisLine: Is {{team}} rebuilding, in a playoff window, or somewhere in between?

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: {{player}} is the franchise guy. We live and die by him.

payload.question: What role does {{player}} have?

options.text: He is the star the team was built around and shoulders a lot of pressure to carry them.
options.explanation: Right. A franchise guy is the player the team is built around, the one fans feel everything through.

options.text: He is a backup and gets limited playing time.
options.explanation: A franchise guy is a star, not a backup. The phrase means the team depends on him heavily for success.

options.text: He is a solid depth player who does his job without carrying the team.
options.explanation: A franchise player is the centerpiece, not a role player. He is likely the highest-paid and gets the most minutes and pressure.

payload.translation: {{player}} is the team's best player and most important piece. The team's success depends heavily on whether he stays healthy and performs at a high level.

followUps.line: How many points or goals is he on pace for this season?
followUps.why: Tracking his production shows whether he is having the elite season fans expect from a franchise player.

followUps.line: Is he under contract for the long term or is he a free agent soon?
followUps.why: Contract status matters for a franchise player. If he is headed for free agency, the team might be in a race to win before he leaves.

payload.prompt: Complete the line about a star player.
payload.template: A team's best, most important player is called its {{label}}, and he usually skates on the {{line}} line.

explanation.correct: Right. The franchise player is the one the team is built around, and he plays on the top line with the most minutes. A healthy scratch is a player sitting out, and an enforcer is a fighting specialist.
explanation.incorrect: The franchise player is the team's centerpiece and skates on the top line. A healthy scratch is a player kept out of the lineup, and an enforcer is a fighting specialist.

payload.prompt: What does it mean when a star player has high time-on-ice (TOI)?

options.text: The player is not trusted by the coach.
The coach relies on the player in tough situations and important moments.
The player is injury-prone and playing through pain.

explanation.correct: Yes. High TOI for a star means the coach is leaning on him. Stars often play the power play and the toughest matchups.
explanation.incorrect: High time on ice is a sign of trust and importance. The coach plays him a lot because he is the best option in crucial moments.

payload.prompt: Match the player role to its description.

pairs.definition: A pure scorer who plays in the offensive zone and finishes scoring chances.
A player who passes and sets up teammates to score, often from the perimeter or point.
A hard-working depth player who checks hard, kills penalties, and does the dirty work.

explanation.summary: Players have different roles based on their skills. A sniper finishes chances, a playmaker sets up teammates, and a grinder does the hard, unglamorous work.
explanation.sayThisLine: Is {{player}} more of a sniper or a playmaker?

payload.prompt: A restricted free agent star: who still holds his rights?

explanation.correct: Right. His team keeps the rights to a restricted free agent. Another club can make an offer, but his team can usually match it, which is why these stars rarely just walk away.
explanation.incorrect: Only an unrestricted free agent can simply sign anywhere. A restricted free agent stays tied to his current team, which can match another club's offer.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We have the worst history against them. Every matchup hurts.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: {{team}} has a poor record against this rival and it stings every time they play.
options.explanation: Right. "History" here means past results, and hers are painful ones.

options.text: Players get injured in games against this team.
options.explanation: A bad history means the teams have played many times with {{team}} losing most. Injury history is a different issue.

options.text: There is drama off the ice between the teams.
options.explanation: On-ice record (wins and losses) is what she is referring to. A 'worst history' means {{team}} keeps losing when it matters.

payload.translation: {{team}} has lost more often than they have won against this rival, and those losses are especially disappointing or memorable.

followUps.line: Is this a recent trend or a long-time thing?
followUps.why: Some rivalries go back decades. Others are new. The age of the rivalry tells you if it is a long-time curse or a recent frustration.

followUps.line: Does {{team}} ever beat them in the playoffs, or is it always the regular season?
followUps.why: If they lose mostly in playoffs, it might be because the rival is better when it matters most.

payload.title: Trash talk and rivalry
payload.setting: Texting after {{team}} loses to their biggest rival.

exchanges.theirMessage: I can't believe we lost to them AGAIN. This rivalry is killing me.

replies.text: That one had to sting. When is the next matchup?
replies.theirResponse: Three weeks. I need to mentally prepare.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledging the pain without piling on shows you get why this matters to her. Asking about next time keeps hope alive.

replies.text: It is just one game. You guys will be fine.
replies.theirResponse: Are you even listening? This rivalry is huge.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her feelings as 'just one game' misses that rivalries carry real emotional weight. It is not just statistics to fans.

replies.text: Their team is so boring anyway. We would crush them in a shootout.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, that is funny. But we still lost.
replies.coachNote: Trashing the rival might feel good, but it does not fix the loss. Stick to genuine sympathy rather than overcompensating with criticism.

payload.closingNote: Rivalries are emotional. Respect that this loss matters more than a regular-season game.

payload.prompt: Her team plays its big rival tonight. Best opener?

options.text: Big one tonight. Do you have a pregame ritual?
It's only two points, right?
Why do you care about this team so much?
Who are they playing again?

explanation.correct: Yes. You know it is a rivalry game and you ask about her own ritual. Rivalry nights are about feeling as much as standings.
explanation.incorrect: Skip the "only two points" take and the blank questions. Show you know the night matters to her, then ask about her own routine.

payload.prompt: Every NHL crowd throws an octopus on the ice for luck.

explanation.correct: False. The octopus is a Detroit Red Wings tradition dating to 1952. Other teams have their own rituals, like goal songs and horns.
explanation.incorrect: Only Detroit fans throw octopi, a tradition from 1952. Every building has its own rituals, which is part of what makes each team's identity.

payload.title: Watch a {{team}} game together
payload.setting: Texting during the first period of a {{team}} game.

exchanges.theirMessage: First line looks sharp tonight. Hope we can get some early goals.

replies.text: They are flying tonight. {{player}} is all over the ice.
replies.theirResponse: I know! He is hungry. We need that energy.
replies.coachNote: Naming a specific observation (like a key player's energy) shows you are watching closely and agree with her read on the game.

replies.theirResponse: Obviously. But the defense needs to tighten up.
replies.coachNote: Generic support is fine but does not deepen the conversation. Notice something specific about the play to show you are engaged.

replies.text: I think the defense looks shaky. They are going to get scored on early.
replies.coachNote: Disagreeing is okay, but it can read as contrarian. Notice what she noticed first, then add your own read.

payload.closingNote: Watching a game together is a chance to notice the same things and share in the emotional ride.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: That is vintage {{team}} hockey right there. Fast break, one-timer, goal.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: That goal reflects {{team}}'s typical playing style and what makes them recognizable.
options.explanation: Right. Here "vintage" is a compliment: that goal is exactly how her team likes to play.

options.text: That is an outdated way to score that {{team}} should not use.
options.explanation: Vintage means characteristic and recognizable, not old or outdated. A fast break and one-timer is a quick, modern way to score.

options.text: They are showing a replay of an old goal from years ago.
options.explanation: Vintage here means it is their signature style happening in real time, not a replay. She is saying 'that is so {{team}}'.

payload.translation: That goal is exactly how {{team}} likes to score: a fast transition and a quick shot. It is the style that defines them.

followUps.why: Understanding the team's identity helps you predict what will frustrate or excite fans. Fast teams love transitions; defensive teams love shutouts.

followUps.line: Is that their strength this season, or are they struggling with pace?
followUps.why: If the team is not matching its identity, it might be due to injuries or coaching changes. That is a common complaint.

payload.prompt: If {{team}} is 'snake-bitten' this season, what does that mean?

options.text: They are playing a defensive or boring style.
They are hitting posts and missing wide on high-quality chances; bad luck.
They have injuries to multiple key players.

explanation.correct: Right. Snake-bitten means they are creating chances but the puck will not go in. Fans usually blame luck, and scoring tends to even out over time.
explanation.incorrect: A snake-bitten team is generating good chances but the puck is not going in. It is not about style or injuries, and fans usually see it as short-term bad luck.

payload.template: A goalie 'standing on his head' is making {{saves}} saves, and fans chirping at a rival are {{act}}.

explanation.correct: Right. 'Standing on his head' is high praise for a goalie stealing a game, and chirping is playful trash talk. Both are classic fan-speak.
explanation.incorrect: A goalie standing on his head is making spectacular saves, and chirping is playful teasing, not leaving or booing.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's standing on his head tonight. They'd be toast without him.
